item.title: Jameel IndexNew Jameel Index release extends horizon to 2050 and integrates climate change and population scenarios to strengthen food security preparedness17 August 2026
item.description:
CAMBRIDGE, MASSACHUSETTS – 17 AUGUST 2026

The Abdul Latif Jameel Water and Food Systems Lab (J-WAFS) at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) released today an expanded version of the Jameel Index for Food Trade and Vulnerability, integrating new climate change and population growth scenarios, and extending its projections to 2050. 

The new version projects food vulnerability across baseline, optimistic, middle, and pessimistic scenarios for all 180+ countries covered by the Jameel Index, and displays predicted vulnerability scores for 2035 and 2050, based on different climate and population models.

The projections can vary significantly: in the Central African Republic, the Jameel Index score rises from 8 in the baseline 2020 model, to 24 in the pessimistic 2050 scenario. For Egypt, a country with a much higher baseline vulnerability of 54, the Jameel Index score rises to 72 in the pessimistic 2050 scenario.

The Jameel Index update marks a shift from a tool that assesses current and near-term food trade vulnerability to one that can project how vulnerability may change as climate and population pressures intensify. 

The new climate and population growth scenarios are mapped to the full suite of indicators available on the Jameel Index platform: food import dependency, animal feed import dependency, food import to export ratio, and supply chain reliability, and robustness. 

Dr Greg Sixt, Project Lead of the Jameel Index, said: “This update to the Jameel Index provides important insight about the impacts of climate change on food security between now and 2050. While a changing climate will impact production in localised areas around the globe, the key factor impacting food security by 2050 is the addition of 1.8 billion mouths to feed, changing diets, and economic growth, especially in low and middle income countries. Therefore trade becomes even more important to meet the growing food demands in low income nations that are being impacted by the changing climate and growing populations.”

Dr Raffaello Cervini, Lead Climate Change Economist at The World Bank, said: “Climate change is redrawing Africa’s map of comparative advantage in food production. With land, water, and labour pulled between food and energy, only integrated, interdisciplinary models can reveal the trade-offs – and whether trade will cushion them or make them worse.”

Dr Linus A. Mofor, Regional Adviser for Sustainability and Climate at UNICEF’s East and Southern Africa Regional Office, said: “The Jameel Index provides a powerful policy support tool for food security and thus human capital development. With increasing impacts of climate change, geopolitical tensions, and consequences for food security, African countries can use the Jameel Index to leverage the African Continental Free Trade Area agreement to better harness the food, trade, and climate nexus for enhanced food security.”

Nader Diab, Head of Programmes at Community Jameel, said: “As the world faces increasing pressure on global food systems, tools that support anticipatory and evidence-based decision-making are becoming increasingly important. Community Jameel is committed to supporting evidence-based policies and solutions, and the expanded Jameel Index will help policymakers and institutions better anticipate risks, strengthen food security, and reduce vulnerability to future shocks.”

The Jameel Index was launched in 2025 to help policymakers, investors, and development practitioners better understand exposure to global food trade risks, synthesising previously isolated food trade indicators into a single composite framework assessing countries’ vulnerability to disruptions across the global food trade network. 

The platform integrates indicators including import dependency, supply chain diversity, supply variability, foreign exchange exposure, and climate change, offering a more holistic understanding of how global trade dynamics influence food security. 

By translating complex trade and climate data into actionable insights, the Jameel Index aims to support more resilient sourcing strategies, policy alignment, and long-term investment planning.

The Jameel Index is the foundational project of the J-WAFS-led Food and Climate Systems Transformation (FACT) Alliance, a global network of more than 20 research institutions and stakeholder organisations working to strengthen resilience across food systems, with support from Community Jameel.

Learn more

Explore the new Jameel Index version: https://jameelindex.mit.edu/future-scenarios

item.title: Community JameelThe Jameel Gallery at the Victoria and Albert Museum celebrates 20 years as a home for one of the world’s most significant Islamic art collections 23 July 2026
item.description:
LONDON – 23 JULY 2026

The Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A), Community Jameel, and Art Jameel today marked the 20th anniversary of The Jameel Gallery at the V&A, celebrating two decades since its opening as a space that has transformed the presentation, interpretation, and public understanding of Islamic art.

Community Jameel marked anniversary with a special reception, hosted at the V&A and attended by HRH Prince Turki Al-Faisal, HRH Prince Abdullah bin Khalid bin Sultan, the Saudi ambassador to the United Kingdom, and Mohammed Jameel KBE, Founder of Community Jameel.

At the event, George Richards, Director of Community Jameel, announced that The Jameel Gallery anniversary celebration had been designated the inaugural event in the official lead-up to the 2029 UK-Saudi Year of Culture.

Opened in July 2006 by HRH The Prince of Wales (as HM King Charles III then was), following a major refurbishment supported by the Jameel family, The Jameel Gallery has revived the V&A’s internationally renowned collection of Islamic art from the Middle East. 

The gallery introduced a new approach to display and interpretation, combining contemporary exhibition design, bespoke cases, lighting, and multimedia resources to help visitors engage more deeply with one of the world’s most significant collections of Islamic art.

The Jameel Gallery at the V&A exhibits more than 400 objects spanning ceramics, textiles, carpets, metalwork, woodwork, glass, and manuscripts, including the Ardabil Carpet, the Minbar of Sultan Qaytbay, and a Fatimid rock crystal ewer. 

Through the gallery, these works are presented not only as historic objects, but as part of a wider story of artistic exchange, craftsmanship, and creativity across the Islamic world.

During the gallery’s refurbishment, the Jameel family supported an international touring exhibition of highlights of the V&A’s collection, to bring them to a wider global audience. 

Between 2004 and 2006, the exhibition, Palace and Mosque: Islamic art from the Victoria and Albert Museum, travelled to the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC; Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth, Texas; Setagaya Art Museum in Tokyo, Japan; and the Millennium Galleries in Sheffield, England.

Over the past 20 years, the partnership between the Jameel family and the V&A has grown beyond the permanent gallery to support contemporary commissions, acquisitions, fellowships, research, public programmes, and digital initiatives aiming to connect historic collections with contemporary artistic practice and new audiences.

A central part of this collaboration is the Jameel Prize, established in 2009 by the V&A as an international award for contemporary art and design inspired by Islamic culture, history, society, and ideas, organised in partnership with Art Jameel. 

Across seven editions, the Jameel Prize has exhibited the work of 63 artists and designers from all over the world, and toured to 22 venues globally. The Prize demonstrates the continuing influence of Islamic cultural traditions on contemporary creative practice.  

Additionally, the Jameel Fellowship Programme provides artists, designers, architects, photographers, and researchers with opportunities to undertake sustained research with the V&A’s collections. 

Residencies are offered to both local and international artists from the Middle East and the diaspora, and give them the opportunity to go behind-the-scenes of the museum, look closely at objects and archives, and develop new lines of enquiry in their practice. 

Fellows have shared their work through displays, performances, and symposia, as well as the Hidden Gems film series, which invites them to discuss a favourite object in The Jameel Gallery. Current Fellow, Adam Rouhana, is working on the V&A’s large collection of photography from Palestine.

The Jameel Gallery has also become a platform for temporary displays and contemporary interventions showcasing the rich traditions of Islamic art. Recent highlights include Tatreez: Palestinian Embroidery, which brings together historic Palestinian dress from the V&A collection with contemporary works by Aya Haidar and Zeid Hijazi, exploring embroidery as both a living artistic tradition and an expression of cultural identity.

To mark The Jameel Gallery’s 20th anniversary, the V&A has curated an extensive programme of activities, including temporary displays, a conference, and public events. Earlier this year, the Museum hosted The Art of Egyptian Khayamiyya, bringing master tentmakers from Cairo’s historic Street of the Tentmakers to the V&A for demonstrations and workshops. 

In June 2026, the V&A opened Golden Threads: Dress from Saudi Arabia, a temporary display in The Jameel Gallery displaying a rare group of early twentieth-century royal garments recently acquired by the V&A and exploring the craftsmanship, regional identity, and cultural significance of Saudi dress.

On 17 July 2026, the V&A hosted The Islamic art museumscape: The Jameel Gallery 20th anniversary conference, bringing together museum professionals, curators, and art historians from leading institutions around the world to discuss how the presentation and interpretation of Islamic art in museums has evolved over the past two decades.

Later this year, as part of the London Design Festival, Aziza Kadyri, a London-based artist of Uzbek descent, will unveil a major new site-specific commission for The Jameel Gallery, drawing on rarely displayed embroidered works from the V&A collection through textile sculptures, hand-embroidered tapestries and interactive digital elements.

Speaking at the anniversary celebration, HRH Prince Turki Al-Faisal said: “As ambassador to Her Majesty the great late Queen Elizabeth II, at which time His Royal Highness the then-Prince of Wales named me chairman of the board of trustees of The [Prince’s] School of Traditional Arts – a privilege and honour that I consider the highest of my ambassadorship. 

“20 years ago, my friend Mohammed Abdul Latif Jameel invited me to attend the inauguration of The Jameel Gallery. Mr Jameel has formed his own endeavours, with many positive developments having occurred since. 

“Under His Majesty King Charles’ stewardship, the relationship between Saudi Arabia and the United Kingdom is flourishing, with His Majesty serving as the principal link between the two countries.”

Fady Jameel, Family Ambassador of Community Jameel and Chairman and Founder of Art Jameel, who attended the reception, said: “The Jameel Gallery at the V&A anchors the Jameel family’s long-standing commitment to supporting and celebrating Islamic art. Over the past 20 years, the gallery has become a platform for research, public engagement, and contemporary creative practice, showing how historic artistic traditions continue to evolve. 

“Through my family’s partnership with the V&A, and Community Jameel’s wider work supporting traditional arts and craftsmanship, we remain committed to fostering partnerships that preserve these traditions, while ensuring they continue to reach new audiences.”

Sir Tristram Hunt, Director of the Victoria and Albert Museum, said: “We remain incredibly grateful to the Jameel family for their visionary support, without which the realisation of The Jameel Gallery at the V&A in 2006 would not have been possible. Now in its 20th year, the Gallery continues to serve as one of the Museum’s most-admired spaces, showcasing 400 objects from our Islamic Middle East collection, free to access for all. 

“The Jameel Programme at the V&A is a deeply valued opportunity to explore and champion art and design from the Middle East and North Africa, and our expert curators are delighted to be delivering enhanced activity for this year, celebrating this important milestone in the history of the Gallery.”

The reception was also attended by Hassan Jameel, Family Ambassador of Community Jameel, Hisham Hamza, and Ghada Alsammanoudi, as well as Emily Cherrington LVO, chief executive officer of The King’s Foundation, a longstanding partner of Community Jameel in supporting the study and practice of the traditional arts. 

Community Jameel’s almost 20-year partnership with The King’s Foundation School of Traditional Arts (KFSTA) includes the Jameel Houses of Traditional Arts, a network of schools for craftsmanship in Cairo, Jeddah and Scotland, on the Dumfries House estate, headquarters of The King’s Foundation. 

The Jameel Gallery anniversary celebration featured live demonstrations of traditional crafts by alumni of the Jameel Houses in Cairo and Jeddah, as well as from KFSTA, including ceramics, wood inlay and gypsum-carving.

Jacqueline Farrell, Executive Director for Education at The King’s Foundation, said: “At The King’s Foundation we have a deep commitment to protecting heritage crafts. For that reason it’s fantastic to be working with Community Jameel on our global initiatives to inspire and teach a new generation in traditional arts skills. 

“It is particularly special to have the Jameel House on-site at our headquarters, Dumfries House, the home of The King's Foundation where we educate over 10,000 students in traditional and sustainable skills every year.”

Community Jameel’s commitment to the traditional arts, with a focus on the Arab world, combines sustaining and continuing historic design and craft practices and providing practical training and job creation opportunities for traditional artists and craftspeople to achieve sustainable livelihoods, a major priority for Community Jameel amid a burgeoning Arab youth employment crisis.

Through The Jameel Gallery and the wider Jameel Programme at the V&A, the partnership continues to support scholarship, cultural exchange, contemporary creativity, and public engagement with the artistic heritage of the Islamic world.

item.title: Jameel Observatory-CREWSnetElfatih Eltahir wins 2026 Arab Water Council Prize14 July 2026
item.description:
JEDDAH, SAUDI ARABIA – 14 JULY 2026

Professor Elfatih Eltahir, lead principal investigator of the Jameel Observatory – Climate Resilience Early Warning System Network (CREWSnet), has won the 2026 Arab Water Council award for creativity and innovation in the field of water sciences for Arab countries, known as the Arab Water Council Prize.

Professor Eltahir, who is His Majesty King Bhumibol Professor of Hydrology and Climate and Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), was awarded first place in the 2026 cycle of the prize at a ceremony in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on 1 July 2026, during the 7th Arab Water Forum, as part of Saudi Water Week.

Awarded periodically by the Non-Conventional Water Resources Platform of the Arab Water Council, a regional organisation, the 2026 prize had the theme Leading climate-resilient water management systems, with a special focus on Arab countries.

In recognising Professor Eltahir, the Arab Water Council acknowledged his contributions to the field, particularly in two key papers:

  • ‘El Niño and natural variability in the flow of the Nile river’, published by Water Resources Research in 1996 (paper)

  • ‘Climate change enhances interannual variability of the Nile river flow’, published by Nature Climate Change in 2017 (paper)

His work identified a teleconnection between El Niño and Nile river flows, providing a foundation for seasonal forecasting of Nile floods and projections of future Nile floods under climate change.

Elfatih Eltahir, His Majesty King Bhumibol Professor of Hydrology and Climate and Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering at MIT, said: “This year 2026, a significant El Niño event is developing in the Pacific Ocean, which is likely to translate into dry conditions over the Nile basin.

“Our research projects that similar events will become more frequent in the future resulting in enhancement of interannual variability of the Nile floods.”

Professor Eltahir received the Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers (PECASE) in the United States in 1997; and the Kuwait Prize in Applied Science in 2000 for his work on climate change.

He was elected as a fellow of the American Geophysical Union (AGU) in 2008 and received the Hydrologic Sciences Award from the AGU in 2017. He was elected as a member of National Academy of Engineering (2023), is a fellow of The World Academy of Sciences (2023), and is a member of the Sudanese National Academy of Sciences.

Leading the Jameel Observatory-CREWSnet

As lead principal investigator of the Jameel Observatory-CREWSnet, Professor Eltahir is spearheading an international effort to transform climate response by developing the world’s first fully integrated system for forecasting climate impacts, supporting proactive decisions and guiding interventions. Its initial focus is on southwest Bangladesh and Sudan.

The Jameel Observatory-CREWSnet recently opened its first Adaptation Fortress in southwest Bangladesh, a novel shelter designed to protect communities from extreme heat and tropical storms.

The first fortress is now ready to host more than 200 people ahead of the summer 2026 hot season.

Co-founded by Community Jameel and MIT, the initiative was launched in 2022 at COP27 in Sharm El Sheikh, Egypt.

One of MIT’s five Climate Grand Challenges flagship projects, the Jameel Observatory-CREWSnet brings together scientists and humanitarians from:

  • MIT, including the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab

  • BRAC, ​​the Bangladesh-founded non-governmental organisation

  • the International Water Management Institute, part of CGIAR

  • the Agricultural Research Corporation in Sudan

In 2024, at COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates (UAE), the Jameel Observatory-CREWSnet was selected as an innovation package by the Agricultural Innovation Mechanism (AIM) for Scale, a joint initiative of the UAE government and the Gates Foundation.

Chaired by Nobel laureate Professor Michael Kremer, AIM for Scale seeks partnership and investment into selected innovation packages.

item.title: Jameel House in CairoMariam Ashraf reimagines the golden mosaics of the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus13 July 2026
item.description:
LONDON – 12 JULY 2026

Gates of Light, a series of gypsum panels by Mariam Ashraf, is featured in the 2026 Degree Show of The King’s Foundation School of Traditional Arts, open from 30 June to 1 August 2026.

In this interview, Mariam introduces one of her panels – The Damascus Gate – which reimagines the golden mosaics of the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus in carved gypsum and gilded glass.

Featuring palm trees, pomegranates, and flowing rivers in a Quranic vision of Paradise, Mariam’s piece incorporates traditional ablaq (alternating black and white masonry) framing and gilding on glass.

Responding to the recent war in Syria – in which craftspeople were killed and displaced, and architectural monuments damaged and destroyed – Mariam shines a light on Syria’s status as one of the oldest, richest centres of traditional Islamic art in the world.

Gates of Light is Mariam’s final project as she graduates from the Master’s programme at The King's Foundation School of Traditional Arts in London.

Previously, Mariam graduated from the two-year programme at the Jameel House of Traditional Arts in Cairo, a collaboration between the The King's Foundation School of Traditional Arts, Community Jameel, and the Cultural Development Fund at the Ministry of Culture in Egypt. 

In 2025, she was selected as one of The King’s Foundation 35 under 35 makers and changemakers. Her artistic mission centres on reviving the vanishing practice of gypsum carving. 

In 2026, Mariam sat on the advisory board of the landmark Leighton House exhibition The Arab Hall: Past and Present, and participated in the show’s public programme, presented by Leighton House and Community Jameel.

So I'm going to take you through my gates, which are actually representing the architecture of Islamic art.

item.title: CLIMAVORE x Jameel at RCACLIMAVORE x Jameel at RCA expands drought-adapted tomato farming in Sicily with grant from the Sicily Environmental Fund7 July 2026
item.description:
PALERMO, SICILY – 6 JULY 2026

CLIMAVORE x Jameel at the Royal College of Art (RCA), an initiative reimagining foodways for drylands and wetlands in the climate crisis, has received a grant from the Sicily Environmental Fund (SEF) to advance its work in strengthening thousands of farmers’ livelihoods in Sicily by supporting the use of drought-resistant varieties adapted to increasingly arid conditions and climate stress.

The grant will expand CLIMAVORE x Jameel at RCA’s support to a network of 45 farms in southern Italy.

Responding to southern Italy’s drought crisis

Southern Italy is currently navigating longer dry seasons and reduced rainfall, pressures that have led to significant drops in agricultural outputs across the southern mainland and islands like Sicily and Sardinia. 

In 2023, extreme weather conditions linked to climate change contributed to a sharp decline in farm productivity, challenging the viability of crops that depend on heavy water usage and external inputs. 

Since its launch in 2024 as a partnership between CLIMAVORE, Community Jameel, and the RCA, CLIMAVORE x Jameel at RCA has supported the planting of over 300,000 drought-resistant seeds through the distribution of 51,000 seedlings to a network of 17,000 growers and households in Italy. 

Through direct partnerships with shops and restaurants and by increasing bulk orders from within and beyond Italy, participating farmers have developed and sold 17 new canned products, including sweet-and-sour zucchini, pickled tomatoes, and dried zucchini, helping to create sustainable livelihoods.

New opportunities for participating farmers

The SEF grant allows CLIMAVORE x Jameel at RCA to expand its footprint by bringing together a cohort of local families and restaurants who have committed to buying directly from farmers. 

By following this model, CLIMAVORE X JAMEEL at RCA creates a guaranteed market for farmers, giving them the financial security to plant a wider variety of seeds. The grant will also fund a community role that will raise awareness around products like tomato passata and engage the restaurants in outreach and showing that farming in dry climates can be both environmental and support local farmers.

Nader Diab, Head of Programmes, Community Jameel, said: "The grant from the Sicily Environmental Fund serves as a significant endorsement of CLIMAVORE x Jameel at RCA’s work  in strengthening and securing farmers’ livelihoods.

"This investment marks a transition from a proven pilot to a regional standard across Sicily, validating a model that supports thousands of farmers while building a framework for climate-resilient agriculture."

Enrico Milazzo, researcher at CLIMAVORE x Jameel at RCA, said: "Expanding the work of CLIMAVORE x Jameel at the Royal College of Art through this grant is an important step in scaling climate-resilient agriculture in Southern Italy. The support of the Sicily Environmental Fund enables the growth of a model that connects farmers more directly with a committed market of local families.

"This investment is key to strengthening agricultural frameworks that protect livelihoods, while building on the success of 17 new product lines and supporting the development of a lasting, water-wise food system across Sicily."

Gaia Agnello, from the Sicilian Environmental Fund, said: "For the Sicilian Environmental Fund, this project and collaboration with CLIMAVORE x Jameel at RCA is important because it addresses policy-relevant challenges while supporting a plurality of farmers and communities across a wide territory in Sicily.

"It is also significant from a biodiversity conservation perspective, as it facilitates cultivation and exchange, building on our previous collaborations with SEF projects. Crucially, it helps foster a market and practical use that more closely connects growers and consumers."

CLIMAVORE x Jameel at RCA’s work in southern Italy is part of the Monoculture Meltdown initiative, collaborating with farmers to develop drought-resilient alternatives to water-intensive monocultures, strengthening agricultural resilience while sustaining local food cultures.

In Türkiye, CLIMAVORE x Jameel at RCA’s Water Buffalo Commons project works with herding communities in the wetlands around Istanbul to support water buffalo pastoralism and sustain threatened ecosystems through traditional dairy practices.

item.title: Jameel InstituteJameel Institute-Realtime Intelligent Support for Emergencies supports Gaza Strip Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment25 June 2026
item.description:
LONDON – 25 JUNE 2026

To support the humanitarian response in Gaza, the Jameel Institute-Realtime Intelligent Support for Emergencies (RISE) programme at Imperial College London contributed research, evidence synthesis, and stakeholder engagement to the Gaza Strip Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA), published by the World Bank, the European Union, and the United Nations.

Dr Paula Christen-Price, a Jameel Institute researcher on secondment to the World Health Organization (WHO), describes how the Jameel Institute-RISE programme supported the assessment, and what an evidence-informed humanitarian response can achieve.

Transcript

The research that we are conducting through the Jameel Institute-RISE programme is the most objective account, and most scientific and unbiased account, of the conflict escalation in the Gaza Strip since 2023.

I am Paula Christen. I am a post-doctoral researcher funded through the Jameel Institute-RISE programme. I am currently on a secondment with the World Health Organization to understand what the actual number of deaths are in the Gaza Strip since the escalation in 2023.

The Jameel Institute-RISE programme has served as a foundation for the damage and needs assessment that most recently took place. The work focuses on how mathematical modelling evidence can be used in humanitarian contexts and crisis settings.

It helped to understand what the baseline requirements are to serve the population in Gaza and to respond to the public health needs – both the chronic diseases as well as infectious diseases that the population is experiencing.

One stream of work is a literature review of all of the evidence that has been developed during responses over the past 10 years in different crisis settings.

The second stream of work is the mathematical model that I’m developing to understand the different causal pathways between the determinants of mortality and how they relate to one another.

And the third stream of work is a focused analysis of the traumatic injuries that have been observed over the year of 2025, to understand whether this increase was statistically significant and can be attributed to the aid distribution.

Beyond violent causes of death, we also observe death due to nonviolent causes – for example, having no access to healthcare services, to nutrition, to water, and hygiene practices.

Together, these streams of work help in informing how public health situation analysis can be conducted.

Of course, no crisis setting is the same. Gaza versus Sudan, they have very different epidemiological profiles to respond to.

However, the determinants that the framework probes on help to understand the critical data needs and how this data can then inform response plans and recovery plans.

Scientific research, in the way that we are doing it in the Jameel Institute-RISE programme, enables an incredibly objective and robust way of looking at a crisis setting – piecemealing all of the different data streams together and building a profound understanding of a crisis situation.

We are developing evidence that is useful for the WHO to run their operations on the ground. So that is resource allocation decisions; those are public health situation analyses which can inform what actions to take next in the humanitarian response, throughout the escalation and also in the recovery planning stages.

As more evidence becomes available through the Jameel Institute-RISE programme and the WHO collaboration, similar tools and evidence should be developed for different crisis types which require a response and humanitarian action that can be done in a lot more evidence-informed way.

I hope that this enables more intelligent and data-driven humanitarian response planning and decision-making processes.

item.title: Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate LabsJameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs showcase enhanced climate planning policies benefitting 4.5 million people to city leaders at London Climate Action Week24 June 2026
item.description:
LONDON – 24 JUNE 2026

4.5 million people at risk of extreme heat, flooding, water stress, and other hazards in the cities of Amman, Jordan, and Chennai, India, will benefit from new climate planning policies implemented by city authorities in collaboration with the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs.

The policies were showcased at an event hosted today by Community Jameel and C40, co-founders of the Jameel C40 Labs, at the London headquarters of design firm Gensler, as part of London Climate Action Week.

Working closely with city governments, planners, and local stakeholders, the Jameel C40 Labs have helped tackle climate risks in Amman and Chennai through planning regulations, master plans, local area plans, neighbourhood frameworks, and other statutory planning instruments, while strengthening the capacity of planners and municipal officials to integrate climate resilience into future decision-making.

The London Climate Action Week event, titled (Re)designing cities and neighbourhoods for a climate-safe future, featured a discussion on how cities can respond to climate change through the way they plan growth, infrastructure, mobility, and public space.

The event comes as cities worldwide face the challenge of accommodating growth, while responding to rising temperatures, worsening air quality, flooding, water scarcity, and increasing pressure on public services. 

Drawing on lessons from the Jameel C40 Labs, the discussion explored how climate evidence can be translated into planning regulations, master plans, neighbourhood projects, and practical tools that shape how cities develop.

The event follows a high-profile presentation, held the day prior at the Bloomberg Local Climate Action Summit, where Uzma Sulaiman, Associate Director of Community Jameel, showcased the work in Amman and Chennai to an audience of over 30 global mayors and 1,100 delegates.

Benefitting 4.5 million people in Amman and Chennai

Established by Community Jameel and C40 to embed climate considerations into urban planning policies, the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs have worked over the past three years in Amman and Chennai, two rapidly growing cities facing different but connected climate pressures. 

Amman has grown from around 5,000 residents a century ago to nearly four million today, while Chennai is managing rapid metropolitan expansion alongside increasing exposure to extreme heat, flooding, and deteriorating air quality. The Jameel C40 Labs initially conducted climate change risk assessments and greenhouse gas inventories to evaluate the risks posed to residents.

In response, the labs have contributed to 15 planning policies, regulations, strategies, and statutory planning instruments across both cities. If fully implemented, these policies are projected to reduce emissions by 26.5 million tonnes of CO₂e annually by the 2040s, equivalent to avoiding the burning of around 11 billion litres of petrol.

The benefits extend beyond climate mitigation. Cleaner air means healthier cities. Air pollution is linked to cardiovascular disease, respiratory illness, and lung cancer. In Jordan, lung cancer represents the nation’s third most prevalent malignancy, with a projected 30% increase in cases over the next ten years as air quality worsens. Similarly, Chennai’s atmosphere has seen a severe decline in air quality alongside intensified traffic, construction, and metropolitan growth.

The Jameel C40 Labs are also helping to shape the forthcoming Master Plans for Amman and Chennai, which together will influence how metropolitan regions with a combined population of more than 14.5 million residents grow in the coming decades. 

Chennai’s Third Master Plan is expected to release its first draft in September 2026, while lessons from the city’s Planning and Zoning Regulations and neighbourhood pilots are helping inform Amman’s future Master Plan, expected to be adopted in 2028.

Translating planning to action

Alongside city-wide planning, the Jameel C40 Labs have translated climate objectives into neighbourhood-scale action in Kherbet Al-Souq, also known as Southern Gate, in Amman, and Madhavaram in Chennai.

In Kherbet Al-Souq, one of Amman’s key future growth areas, the Jameel C40 Labs supported a plan for a neighbourhood expected to grow from around 25,000 residents today to 42,000 by 2050.

Completed and handed over to the Greater Amman Municipality in May 2026, the plan provides a framework for accommodating growth while protecting cultivated landscapes, reducing infrastructure pressures, improving mobility, expanding access to services and public space, and strengthening climate resilience.

Building on this work, the Jameel C40 Labs are collaborating with Sanabel, a landscape architecture and urban design firm, on a tactical urbanism pilot project in Al Yarmook neighbourhood in Amman. Due to be completed and inaugurated in August 2026, the pilot marks an important transition from planning to implementation. 

The Al Yarmook pilot will test climate-responsive public-space improvements before larger investments are made, including shaded gathering areas, drought-tolerant planting, urban greening, pedestrian-safety measures, and nature-based cooling solutions tailored to Amman’s climate. 

The pilot will also show how simple and affordable interventions can reduce urban heat, improve walkability, encourage social interaction, make streets safer for communities, and create more comfortable public spaces during increasingly hot summers.

In Madhavaram, Chennai, the Jameel C40 Labs are supporting a pilot to redesign the built environment to better address flooding, heat and environmental degradation. Studies estimate that future flood damage in the city could reach up to USD 10 billion if urban growth continues to undermine flood resilience.

The plan combines mobility, public space and nature-based solutions, including ecological restoration, blue-green infrastructure and improved water management, to support a more resilient and liveable neighbourhood. 

As Chennai prepares to adopt its Third Master Plan, the pilot provides a practical example of how climate objectives can be translated into neighbourhood-scale projects and investment priorities.

Nader Diab, Head of Programmes, Community Jameel, said: "As cities face increasing climate risks, actionable planning policies are essential to improving quality of life and strengthening climate resilience for residents.

"Through close collaboration with city authorities in Amman and Chennai and guided by community priorities, the Jameel C40 Labs have helped translate climate evidence into policies, neighbourhood projects and practical tools that support more climate-safe urban development.

"We are pleased that the lessons from this work are now informing the C40 and UN-Habitat Urban Planning Accelerator, helping extend this approach to cities around the world."

Hélène Chartier, Director of Urban Planning and Design, C40 Cities, said: "Urban planning is one of the most powerful tools cities have to combat the climate crisis. What we have achieved through the Jameel C40 Labs in Amman and Chennai proves that when we embed climate evidence directly into everyday zoning laws, master plans, and neighborhood designs, the benefits to emissions reductions, climate resilience, public health and the local environment are immense.

"By taking these proven, data-driven approaches and scaling them globally through the Urban Planning Accelerator, we are empowering planners worldwide to fundamentally redesign our cities for a safer, more livable future."

Climate action through community engagement

Participation and shared ownership have been central to the Jameel C40 Labs’ approach to enhanced planning. Through community consultations, stakeholder workshops, and neighbourhood visioning exercises, local priorities have shaped planning decisions in both cities.

Through the Jameel C40 Students Reinventing Cities Challenge, more than 170 university students from Jordan, Egypt, and Italy developed proposals for the future of Kherbet Al-Souq, exploring how mobility, public space, water management, urban greening and climate resilience could be integrated into one of Amman’s most important future growth areas.

Building on this work, Jameel C40 Schools Reinventing Amman is engaging around 400 school students through Minecraft Education, inviting them to redesign public spaces in Kherbet Al-Souq and explore challenges including urban farming, food security, public space, and climate resilience.

The initiative will conclude in August 2026, with selected proposals shared with the Greater Amman Municipality, giving young people a voice in shaping the future of their city.

The Jameel C40 Labs have also produced practical knowledge products, including the Climate Action Guide for Urban Planners, which translates lessons from the programme into tools that help planners integrate climate action into plans, regulations and development decisions. A dedicated India edition of the guide is set to be released soon, helping planners across the country apply climate action in urban planning practice.

The work produced by the Jameel C40 Labs has also laid the foundations for the C40 and UN-Habitat Urban Planning Accelerator, launched at COP30 in Brazil in 2025, which is now supporting 33 cities globally and scaling approaches first developed through the labs, including Amman, the home city where this approach was piloted, as well as Jeddah, Accra, Buenos Aires, Cape Town, Madrid, and Nairobi, among others, with Chennai set to join in the near future.

Completed and handed over to the Greater Amman Municipality in May 2026, the plan provides a framework for accommodating growth while protecting cultivated landscapes, reducing infrastructure pressures, improving mobility, expanding access to services and public space, and strengthening climate resilience.

Building on this work, the Jameel C40 Labs are collaborating with Sanabel, a landscape architecture and urban design firm, on a tactical urbanism pilot project in Al Yarmook neighbourhood in Amman. Due to be completed and inaugurated in August 2026, the pilot marks an important transition from planning to implementation. 

The Al Yarmook pilot will test climate-responsive public-space improvements before larger investments are made, including shaded gathering areas, drought-tolerant planting, urban greening, pedestrian-safety measures, and nature-based cooling solutions tailored to Amman’s climate. 

The pilot will also show how simple and affordable interventions can reduce urban heat, improve walkability, encourage social interaction, make streets safer for communities, and create more comfortable public spaces during increasingly hot summers.

In Madhavaram, Chennai, the Jameel C40 Labs are supporting a pilot to redesign the built environment to better address flooding, heat and environmental degradation. Studies estimate that future flood damage in the city could reach up to USD 10 billion if urban growth continues to undermine flood resilience.

The plan combines mobility, public space and nature-based solutions, including ecological restoration, blue-green infrastructure and improved water management, to support a more resilient and liveable neighbourhood. 

As Chennai prepares to adopt its Third Master Plan, the pilot provides a practical example of how climate objectives can be translated into neighbourhood-scale projects and investment priorities.

Nader Diab, Head of Programmes, Community Jameel, said: "As cities face increasing climate risks, actionable planning policies are essential to improving quality of life and strengthening climate resilience for residents.

"Through close collaboration with city authorities in Amman and Chennai and guided by community priorities, the Jameel C40 Labs have helped translate climate evidence into policies, neighbourhood projects and practical tools that support more climate-safe urban development.

"We are pleased that the lessons from this work are now informing the C40 and UN-Habitat Urban Planning Accelerator, helping extend this approach to cities around the world."

Hélène Chartier, Director of Urban Planning and Design, C40 Cities, said: "Urban planning is one of the most powerful tools cities have to combat the climate crisis. What we have achieved through the Jameel C40 Labs in Amman and Chennai proves that when we embed climate evidence directly into everyday zoning laws, master plans, and neighborhood designs, the benefits to emissions reductions, climate resilience, public health and the local environment are immense.

"By taking these proven, data-driven approaches and scaling them globally through the Urban Planning Accelerator, we are empowering planners worldwide to fundamentally redesign our cities for a safer, more livable future."

Climate action through community engagement

Participation and shared ownership have been central to the Jameel C40 Labs’ approach to enhanced planning. Through community consultations, stakeholder workshops, and neighbourhood visioning exercises, local priorities have shaped planning decisions in both cities.

Through the Jameel C40 Students Reinventing Cities Challenge, more than 170 university students from Jordan, Egypt, and Italy developed proposals for the future of Kherbet Al-Souq, exploring how mobility, public space, water management, urban greening and climate resilience could be integrated into one of Amman’s most important future growth areas.

Building on this work, Jameel C40 Schools Reinventing Amman is engaging around 400 school students through Minecraft Education, inviting them to redesign public spaces in Kherbet Al-Souq and explore challenges including urban farming, food security, public space, and climate resilience.

The initiative will conclude in August 2026, with selected proposals shared with the Greater Amman Municipality, giving young people a voice in shaping the future of their city.

The Jameel C40 Labs have also produced practical knowledge products, including the Climate Action Guide for Urban Planners, which translates lessons from the programme into tools that help planners integrate climate action into plans, regulations and development decisions. A dedicated India edition of the guide is set to be released soon, helping planners across the country apply climate action in urban planning practice.

item.title: Jameel Arts & Health LabHealing Arts takes centre stage in Ukraine's response to war trauma 23 June 2026
item.description:
LVIV, UKRAINE – 23 JUNE 2026

Art Therapy Force, the Jameel Arts & Health Lab, the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Europe, and King's College London launched Healing Arts Ukraine today, showcasing the arts as critical human infrastructure in times of war.

Ukraine is facing a mental health emergency that its healthcare system cannot meet on its own. 93% of the Ukrainian population reports symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) or stress, yet only one in four of those who seek support are able to get it.

Healing Arts Ukraine, launched in Lviv this week, has been built directly in response to this shortfall, treating creative health not as a comfort but as a working part of the country’s health response.

Healing Arts Ukraine forms part of the Jameel Arts & Health Lab’s global Healing Arts campaign, developed in collaboration with the WHO. The initiative is being led locally by Art Therapy Force, with support from the European Union-funded Health Resilience in the Eastern Partnership programme.

The 2026 programme builds on the success of Healing Arts Lviv, held in 2025. This year’s campaign combines a training school for practitioners, a congress exploring the integration of the arts into formal healthcare delivery, and 20 free public events across Lviv.

Together, these activities aim to support the development of evidence-informed arts and health policy in Ukraine and contribute to the integration of arts-based approaches within the country’s healthcare system.

The treatment gap

As of early 2026, some 239 million people worldwide needed urgent humanitarian assistance, and Ukraine’s own crisis sits within that wider picture. The country saw a 20 percent rise in attacks on healthcare infrastructure in 2025 alone, pushing conventional medical support further out of reach for the people who need it most. Arts-based care has stepped into that space, not as an alternative but as one of the few options still standing in some areas. 

Veronika Skliarova, founder, Art Therapy Force, said: "Ukraine is home to a growing number of organisations, institutions, and practitioners working at the intersection of arts and health. These practices are becoming a powerful driver of change: the arts offer new ways of responding to crises, while creative practice opens pathways for processing traumatic experiences, rebuilding social connections, and fostering psychological resilience."

Iryna Holubetska, from the Unbroken Foundation in Lviv, said: "The war in Ukraine is impacting our minds, our bodies, and our social fabric every day. Arts-based approaches are allowing people to process trauma in ways that conventional approaches often cannot. Integrating the arts into health systems is not a luxury in wartime – it is an essential part of recovery and resilience."

Christopher Bailey, global policy lead, Jameel Arts & Health Lab, said: "War doesn’t just destroy infrastructure, physical safety, and national security. It also impacts on the psychological welfare of soldiers and civilians experiencing danger and hardship. Addressing mental health in such contexts requires a mobilisation of ways to sustain social bonds, soothe emotional collapse, find ways of co-creating meaning, and bring hope."

Practitioners delivering these programmes are also pushing back on the idea that the work is supplementary. Ostap Ukrainets of Cultural Forces described culture as "a wartime resource that offers support across frontline and home front experiences. The programmes that Cultural Forces delivers are not mere entertainments; they are targeted clinical interventions to reduce combat stress and prevent the onset of acute PTSD".  

From response to policy 

Healing Arts Ukraine partly grew out of a roundtable held earlier this year in London at the Houses of Parliament, where defence and cultural policymakers sat alongside WHO officials, military personnel, non-governmental organisations, clinicians, and artists to discuss the arts’ role in military health, veteran recovery, and civilian resilience. That cross-sector mix is now shaping the design of the Lviv programme itself. 

The centrepiece of Healing Arts Ukraine 2026 is a school built on the Trauma-Attuned Arts Framework developed by clinical psychologist Angela Kennedy, trauma therapy specialist Darren Abrahams, King’s College London war studies lecturer Henry Redwood, and producer Veronika Skliarova, working alongside Ukrainian experts.

It will train artists, psychologists, and health and social workers in trauma-attuned practice through lectures, workshops, and group work, alongside a congress on implementing an arts-on-prescription model. 

Art Therapy Force is bringing Ukrainian government ministries into that conversation directly, alongside doctors and arts and health professionals already involved. Healing Arts Ukraine provides the space for turning all of the existing arts and health activity into a recognised driver of recovery and policy, rather than a parallel, informal effort. 

Arts and culture have played a key role in navigating adversity throughout human history, but this is now being backed up by a robust scientific evidence base. This research provides key learning about the vital role the arts in times of war, which is transferable to other humanitarian settings and traumas. 

Veronica Skliarova, founder, Art Therapy Force, added: "In the wake of mass displacement and war-related trauma, the arts have become a crucial instrument for recovery, offering communities a non-verbal pathway to process experiences of loss with resilience and participatory tools."

item.title: Jameel Arts & Health LabNicola Benedetti named first Global Ambassador for Healing Arts by the Jameel Arts & Health Lab20 June 2026
item.description:
EDINBURGH – 20 JUNE 2026

Violinist Nicola Benedetti has been named the first ever Global Ambassador for Healing Arts by the Jameel Arts & Health Lab, the global centre established by the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Europe, the Steinhardt School at New York University, Community Jameel, and CULTURUNNERS, with a mission to measurably improve health and wellbeing through the arts. 

The appointment was announced ahead of Healing Arts Scotland 2026, the world's largest biennial celebration of the arts and health, where Benedetti joined the national Healing Arts Scotland conference at the National Galleries of Scotland.

As Global Ambassador, Benedetti will advocate on behalf of the Jameel Arts & Health Lab for the integration of the arts into mainstream healthcare to audiences, practitioners, and policymakers worldwide. 

Healing Arts Scotland is part of the Jameel Arts & Health Lab’s global Healing Arts campaign, in collaboration with WHO. The first edition in 2024 deployed 376 events nationwide, culminating in an impact report presented at the Scottish Parliament that actively influenced national public health policy.

The 2026 expansion was scaled with five regional flagship days and a national conference in Edinburgh, alongside a week of talks, exhibitions, performances, and workshops across the country.

A voice for the arts in health

Benedetti brings to the role a career that has paired artistic excellence with sustained public advocacy. Born in West Kilbride, Scotland, in 1987, she began playing the violin at the age of four and rose to national prominence in 2004 when, aged 16, she won BBC Young Musician of the Year, performing Szymanowski's Violin Concerto No. 1.

In September 2012, she performed at the Last Night of the Proms, playing Bruch's Violin Concerto No. 1. She is a Grammy Award winner, founder of the Benedetti Foundation, and the first woman and the first Scot to lead the Edinburgh International Festival as director.

Nicola Benedetti, Global Ambassador for Healing Arts at the Jameel Arts & Health Lab, said: "Through my work with the Edinburgh International Festival, I see every day the profound role that artistic experiences can play in bringing people together, opening space for reflection and fostering a sense of belonging."

Healing Arts Scotland is spearheaded by a coalition of organisations bridging culture, healthcare, education, and policy, including the Scottish Government, Public Health Scotland, Creative Scotland, the National Galleries Scotland, Scottish Ballet, Arts Culture Health & Wellbeing Scotland, the International Teaching Artists Collaborative, and the National Health Service Scotland.

item.title: Jameel Observatory-CREWSnetJameel Observatory-CREWSnet opens first Adaptation Fortress in Bangladesh during El Niño heat extremes18 June 2026
item.description:
SATKHIRA, BANGLADESH - 18 JUNE 2026

The Jameel Observatory – Climate Resilience Early Warning System Network (CREWSnet) has opened its first Adaptation Fortress, a novel shelter designed to protect communities from extreme heat and tropical storms in southwest Bangladesh, ready to host 200 people ahead of the summer 2026 hot season.

Developed by the Jameel Observatory-CREWSnet, an initiative co-founded by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Community Jameel, in partnership with BRAC, the Bangladesh-founded non-governmental organisation, the Adaptation Fortress transforms the traditional concept of a cyclone shelter at the Baradal Aftab Uddin Collegiate School in the Satkhira district into a permanent, year-round community asset that for the first time offers protection to residents from two of the region’s most severe and growing climate threats.

During heat waves in this region, temperatures can reach 44°C. At these levels, the body’s natural cooling mechanisms suffer significantly, making the Adaptation Fortress’ climate-controlled sanctuary essential to preventing heatstrokes, especially among the elderly.

For the 30 million residents of southwestern Bangladesh, who face a compounding cycle of cyclones and record-breaking heatwaves, this pilot represents a milestone in the transition from reactive disaster management to proactive, evidence-based protection.

Ready for the hot season

The opening comes as climate projections indicate a severe El Niño pattern in 2026, which will intensify heat extremes and increase the frequency and severity of climate shocks worldwide, elevating risks of prolonged heatwaves and compounding climate stressors which may further exacerbate risks to the local population.

The Adaptation Fortress is fully operational ahead of the summer season in 2026, providing cooled shelter and clean water to some of Bangladesh’s most vulnerable residents.

The urgency for this infrastructure follows the record-breaking 2024 heatwave, which forced a nationwide shutdown of the education system, affecting 33 million students.

A community-led sanctuary

To ensure that the Adaptation Fortress serves those most at risk, a priority access list has been established, focusing on the elderly, individuals with respiratory conditions such as asthma, expectant mothers and mothers with infants, and students of the school where the shelter is hosted.

Day-to-day operations and emergency protocols will be overseen by the school committee in partnership with BRAC, formalised through a signed memorandum of understanding to ensure long-term sustainability. The facility is supported by a comprehensive user guide, translated into Bangla, to empower local management.

During government-declared heat emergencies, the facility is equipped to host up to 200 people, providing a climate-controlled space and filtered water. In its capacity as a reinforced cyclone shelter, the structure can host up to 500 people, offering high-ground safety.

Engineered for resilience

The infrastructure of the pilot Adaptation Fortress is designed for maximum durability. The facility is powered by a rooftop solar array and battery backup system that ensures it remains fully operational during grid failure, precisely when it is needed most.

To combat extreme heat, the building features solar-grid based air conditioning units. The windows of the building are made of glass with iron cases to protect from breakage in a school environment, and maintain insulation of the climate-controlled rooms.

Water security is integrated into the facility through the Rain for Life project, a partnership between BRAC and the Danish Embassy in Dhaka that provides safe, climate-resilient drinking water by installing large-scale rainwater harvesting systems, mitigating the severe salinity intrusion that plagues local groundwater sources.

In addition, a net-metering interface is installed that allows surplus electricity generated during periods of low occupancy to be sold back into the national grid, creating a circular revenue stream that funds long-term maintenance and reduces dependence on external funding.

This first pilot Adaptation Fortress opens the path for a broader regional rollout of the Jameel Observatory-CREWSnet model. Performance will be rigorously assessed through remote sensors tracking temperature, humidity and power consumption alongside a manual registration book.

These insights will directly inform the construction of a second Adaptation Fortress at Satbaria High School in the Jashore district of southwestern Bangladesh, scheduled to begin before the end of 2026

If successful, this evidence-based pathway opens a trajectory for scaling to 1,250 Adaptation Fortresses across the region, providing permanent heat and storm relief to hundreds of thousands of its most vulnerable residents.

item.title: Community JameelV&A opens Golden Threads, a new temporary display exploring traditional Saudi dress, now on view in The Jameel Gallery at V&A South Kensington16 June 2026
item.description:
LONDON – 16 JUNE 2026

The Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) has opened Golden Threads: Dress from Saudi Arabia, a special temporary display of mid-twentieth-century traditional dress from Saudi Arabia, now on view in The Jameel Gallery at V&A South Kensington. Running until 30 May 2027 and free to visit, the display is part of the V&A’s Jameel Programme, celebrating 20 years of The Jameel Gallery with Community Jameel.

In 1932, Abdulaziz bin Abdul Rahman Al Saud (also known as Ibn Saud) founded the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. During his reign, King Abdulaziz followed the long-standing Islamic tradition of rulers presenting fine garments as gifts, including to foreign visitors. He gave the luxurious outfits included in the display to the daughter of Sir Hugh Stonehewer Bird, the British Ambassador to Saudi Arabia, in 1942 and 1952.

Traditional dress in Saudi Arabia varies enormously across the country. The colourful and voluminous examples on display are all from the central Najd region, where King Abdulaziz and the Saud family are from. They would have been worn for weddings and other special occasions.

However, while these styles are rooted in Najd, their materials and embroidery techniques reveal wider global connections, especially with India. The garments are all embellished with metal-wrapped thread that catches the light with a golden shimmer. Recently acquired by the V&A through a donation from Sir Hugh Stonehewer Bird’s family, this collection of garments preserves an important example of Saudi textile heritage and makes it accessible to international audiences through the Museum's collection and public programme. 

Focusing on dress traditions associated with the Najd region, the historic homeland of the Saud family, the display offers visitors insight into the ceremonial life, material culture and textile heritage of central Saudi Arabia during the early decades of the Kingdom's formation.

Fuchsia Hart, Sarikhani Curator, V&A, said: "The V&A is delighted to be displaying these remarkable garments from Saudi Arabia, which were generously gifted to the museum in 2025 by the family of Sir Hugh Stonehewer Bird. They reveal not only the vibrancy of traditional dress from the Kingdom, but also highlight the international connections which shaped Najdi thobes and the role they played in royal gifting practices."

Nader Diab, Head of Programmes at Community Jameel, said: "As we celebrate 20 years of The Jameel Gallery at the V&A, Community Jameel is proud to see a rich display of historic dress from Saudi Arabia, the home of the Jameel family, offering a rare opportunity to explore an important aspect of the Kingdom's heritage, while celebrating the craftsmanship, creativity and cultural exchange embodied in these remarkable garments. We are pleased to continue our relationship with the V&A in supporting initiatives that deepen understanding of the artistic and cultural traditions of the Islamic world.” 

Antonia Carver, Director of Art Jameel, said: "The Jameel Gallery was conceived as a place of discovery in the centre of London where audiences can encounter the histories and material cultures of the Islamic world in a contemporary museum context. The compelling temporary displays in the Jameel Gallery, including this rare chance to delve into the history of Saudi dress, draw on archival research and scholarship to explore how objects convey stories of identity and exchange – from embroidered textiles to garments and everyday artefacts."

Extensively refurbished with support from the Jameel family and opened in 2006 by HM The King (as The Prince of Wales), The Jameel Gallery is one of the V&A’s principal galleries and houses more than 400 objects spanning ceramics, textiles, carpets, metalwork, woodwork, glass and manuscripts from across the Islamic world, dating from the eighth century to the present day. Through its displays, exhibitions and public programmes, the Gallery has served as a platform for cultural exchange, scholarship, conservation and public engagement.

The display echoes Art Jameel’s own wider engagement with cultural heritage and contemporary creative practice in Saudi Arabia, including at Hayy Jameel, Jeddah, Art Jameel’s flagship creative complex and platform for exhibitions, learning and community programmes. The Jameel Programme at the V&A also includes the Museum’s triennial Jameel Prize, in partnership with Art Jameel, an award for contemporary art and design inspired by Islamic art, culture, history, society and ideas. 

Community Jameel's broader work in the field of traditional dress includes Costumes Populaires Reimagined, a digital initiative that revisits a celebrated nineteenth-century photographic archive of traditional dress from the Middle East and North Africa, through colourisation, animation and artificial intelligence technologies, helping bring historic textile traditions and regional identities to new audiences.

Recently acquired by the V&A through a donation from Sir Hugh Stonehewer Bird’s family, this collection of garments preserves an important example of Saudi textile heritage and makes it accessible to international audiences through the Museum's collection and public programme. 

Focusing on dress traditions associated with the Najd region, the historic homeland of the Saud family, the display offers visitors insight into the ceremonial life, material culture and textile heritage of central Saudi Arabia during the early decades of the Kingdom's formation.

Fuchsia Hart, Sarikhani Curator, V&A, said: "The V&A is delighted to be displaying these remarkable garments from Saudi Arabia, which were generously gifted to the museum in 2025 by the family of Sir Hugh Stonehewer Bird. They reveal not only the vibrancy of traditional dress from the Kingdom, but also highlight the international connections which shaped Najdi thobes and the role they played in royal gifting practices."

Nader Diab, Head of Programmes at Community Jameel, said: "As we celebrate 20 years of The Jameel Gallery at the V&A, Community Jameel is proud to see a rich display of historic dress from Saudi Arabia, the home of the Jameel family, offering a rare opportunity to explore an important aspect of the Kingdom's heritage, while celebrating the craftsmanship, creativity and cultural exchange embodied in these remarkable garments. We are pleased to continue our relationship with the V&A in supporting initiatives that deepen understanding of the artistic and cultural traditions of the Islamic world.” 

Antonia Carver, Director of Art Jameel, said: "The Jameel Gallery was conceived as a place of discovery in the centre of London where audiences can encounter the histories and material cultures of the Islamic world in a contemporary museum context. The compelling temporary displays in the Jameel Gallery, including this rare chance to delve into the history of Saudi dress, draw on archival research and scholarship to explore how objects convey stories of identity and exchange – from embroidered textiles to garments and everyday artefacts."

Extensively refurbished with support from the Jameel family and opened in 2006 by HM The King (as The Prince of Wales), The Jameel Gallery is one of the V&A’s principal galleries and houses more than 400 objects spanning ceramics, textiles, carpets, metalwork, woodwork, glass and manuscripts from across the Islamic world, dating from the eighth century to the present day. Through its displays, exhibitions and public programmes, the Gallery has served as a platform for cultural exchange, scholarship, conservation and public engagement.

The display echoes Art Jameel’s own wider engagement with cultural heritage and contemporary creative practice in Saudi Arabia, including at Hayy Jameel, Jeddah, Art Jameel’s flagship creative complex and platform for exhibitions, learning and community programmes. The Jameel Programme at the V&A also includes the Museum’s triennial Jameel Prize, in partnership with Art Jameel, an award for contemporary art and design inspired by Islamic art, culture, history, society and ideas. 

Community Jameel's broader work in the field of traditional dress includes Costumes Populaires Reimagined, a digital initiative that revisits a celebrated nineteenth-century photographic archive of traditional dress from the Middle East and North Africa, through colourisation, animation and artificial intelligence technologies, helping bring historic textile traditions and regional identities to new audiences.

item.title: Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate LabsCity of Jeddah joins global C40 x UN-Habitat Urban Planning Accelerator, building on Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs 15 June 2026
item.description:
JEDDAH, SAUDI ARABIA – 15 JUNE 2026

Jeddah, Saudi Arabia’s second city, has joined the Urban Planning Accelerator, a global initiative for climate-responsive urban planning launched by the United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-Habitat) and C40 Cities, a global network of nearly 100 mayors driving the future of city climate action.

The Urban Planning Accelerator builds on the partnerships and practical approaches of the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, established in 2023 by C40 and Community Jameel to support cities in translating sustainable urban planning into concrete, implementable policies and action on the ground. 

Accelerating urban action in the face of climate stress

Cities across South and West Asia face extreme heat, water stress and rapid urbanisation. In Jeddah, these risks are further compounded by fast urban growth along the vulnerable Red Sea coastline.

By joining the accelerator, alongside 32 global cities, Jeddah aims to fast-track climate-responsive urban planning to prioritise people, the planet, and shared prosperity. Community Jameel Saudi established initial contact between the Jameel C40 Labs and Jeddah Municipality.

The Urban Planning Accelerator supports cities in developing more resilient and sustainable urban environments. It provides practical guidance for mayors and city planners on reducing emissions, adapting to climate risks and restoring ecosystems. The programme encourages compact, connected, and people-centred cities that are healthier, more resilient, and easier to navigate. 

Building on the work of the Jameel C40 Labs

A key resource for participating cities is the work generated by the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, which have guided planning decisions benefitting more than 4 million people in Amman, Jordan, and Chennai, India. The labs have supported policymakers in shaping statutory planning documents, zoning regulations, and investment priorities; providing detailed greenhouse gas inventories; climate risk assessments; and other evidence-based tools. 

This work is expected to reduce millions of tonnes of emissions over the coming decades while lowering exposure to climate risks such as extreme heat and flooding in both Amman and Chennai.

The Jameel C40 Labs’ methodologies and insights are now being scaled globally through the Accelerator, allowing participating cities, including Jeddah, to leverage climate data, analytical tools and knowledge-sharing platforms developed by the labs and adopt and replicate proven solutions within their local contexts. 

Jeddah and other cities joining the Accelerator will also utilise the Climate Action Guide for Urban Planners, which was developed by the Jameel C40 Labs’ co-founders C40 and Community Jameel, in partnership with UrbanShift.

The guide, which was launched at the 12th World Urban Forum in Cairo, Egypt, in November 2024, provides a practical framework for embedding climate action across all stages of urban plan preparation.

Jeddah Municipality stated: "Joining the Urban Planning Accelerator represents a pivotal step in Jeddah’s journey toward a sustainable and resilient future. By integrating the evidence-based methodologies developed through the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, we are ensuring that our city’s rapid growth is matched by a sophisticated, climate-responsive strategy.

"In line with Saudi Vision 2030, this collaboration allows us to safeguard our unique Red Sea coastline and enhance the quality of life for all residents through urban planning that prioritizes people, health, and environmental stewardship."

Nader Diab, Head of Programmes, Community Jameel, said: “We are pleased to see the city of Jeddah join the Urban Planning Accelerator. As the home of the Jameel family, this is a significant milestone for us at Community Jameel and marks a continuation of the work developed through the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs.

"By helping connect cities with initiatives such as the accelerator, we aim to bridge the gap between local municipalities and the resources and networks needed to adopt evidence-informed approaches to sustainable urban planning."

Hélène Chartier, Director of Urban Planning and Design, C40, said: "Urban planning is climate action, and Jeddah’s participation in the Accelerator reflects a strong commitment to leadership. By joining this network of ambitious cities, Jeddah will both draw on global best practices and share its own valuable insights on adapting planning approaches and policies to address climate challenges.

"We look forward to working closely with the Municipality to build on the foundations of the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs and to help deliver a more sustainable, resilient, and liveable future for all of Jeddah’s residents."

Dr May Taibah, member of the board of trustees, Community Jameel Saudi, said: “Saudi cities are on the front lines of climate action, as they act as hubs for innovation and collective action. By helping to facilitate this initiative, Community Jameel Saudi reinforces its commitment to the Saudi Vision 2030 goals of scaling science-led solutions that protect urban lives and livelihoods. Our goal is to ensure that the world’s cities grow, and bridge the gap between global research and local impact.”

Supporting Jeddah's development

Over the coming decade, Jeddah’s engagement in the Accelerator will support key priorities under its strategic and structural plans, in line with Saudi Vision 2030, which will guide redevelopment, transit-oriented development and flood risk management.

These plans will also support the development of more compact and connected neighbourhoods; protection of areas at high climate risk; preservation of land for nature; and the inclusion of affordable housing.

Technical guidance and access to best practices through the Accelerator and its resources will ensure that these plans are evidence-informed and climate-responsive. 

Jeddah joins 32 other cities participating in the accelerator, namely Accra, Cape Town, Dar es Salaam, Thekwini/Durban, Freetown, Johannesburg, Nairobi, Tshwane, Jakarta, Quezon City, Tokyo, Athens, Barcelona, Copenhagen, Istanbul, Madrid, Milan, Paris, Bogotá, Buenos Aires, Curitiba, Fortaleza, Guadalajara, Lima, Medellín, Quito, Rio de Janeiro, Chicago, Portland, Vancouver, Amman and Karachi.
